patient.chief_complaint: Progressive speech difficulty and swallowing problems over 7 months with arm weakness
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. P is a 65-year-old right-handed retired accountant who presents with a 7-month history of progressive dysarthria and dysphagia. He initially noticed his speech becoming slurred and soft approximately 7 months ago, which he attributed to dry mouth from his medications. He himself noted that his voice had changed quality, becoming nasal and strained, and this was also remarked upon by his adult children during visits. Over the past 4-5 months, he has had increasing difficulty swallowing solid foods and has had multiple episodes of coughing after drinking thin liquids.

Concurrently, he has noticed progressive bilateral arm weakness over the past 5 months. He has difficulty opening jars, cutting food, and typing on his computer. He has noticed visible twitching in his arms and has developed painful cramps in his hands and forearms at night. His son has also noted twitching in his tongue.

He has a background of atrial fibrillation and his cardiologist initially considered whether an embolic TIA could explain some symptoms, but the progressive course over months does not fit a vascular etiology. Brain MRI performed by his cardiologist showed no infarct but did show some subtle changes in the corticospinal tracts which prompted neurology referral. He has mild lower extremity weakness noted on examination by his internist 3 months ago, which has not clearly progressed. He has no sensory symptoms, no diplopia, and no bladder or bowel changes.

He lives alone since his wife's passing 2 years ago and is concerned about his ability to manage independently. His son has been helping with meal preparation.

specialized_test.impression: Active denervation (fibrillations, positive sharp waves) and chronic reinnervation (large amplitude, long duration, polyphasic MUPs, reduced recruitment) are present in the bulbar, cervical, and thoracic body regions, with early lumbosacral involvement. Sensory NCS are normal. Reduced CMAP amplitudes with preserved conduction velocities. No conduction block. Findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, bulbar-onset, clinically definite

differential.key_features: PLS has pure UMN involvement; EMG here shows active LMN denervation (fibrillations) in bulbar, cervical, thoracic regions — PLS excluded
Bulbar findings above level of any cervical pathology; MRI shows no cord signal change
No fatigable weakness, no diplopia, EMG shows denervation not decrement; MG does not cause fasciculations or hyperreflexia
Progressive 7-month course inconsistent with vascular event; no DWI change on MRI; bilateral multi-region findings inconsistent with single vascular territory

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral corticospinal tract signal change, no infarct (important given anticoagulation)
Denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic regions

optimal_actions.action: Pulmonary function — urgent given FVC approaching threshold
Modified barium swallow study given aspiration risk
Drug interaction check for riluzole with anticoagulation

critical_actions: Urgent pulmonary function testing — FVC 68% and SNIP near threshold requires immediate NIV planning
Swallowing evaluation — silent aspiration identified, diet modification prevents aspiration pneumonia
Initiate riluzole — check interactions with anticoagulation first
PEG tube discussion at FVC 68% — must be placed before FVC falls below 50% for safety
EMG including bulbar region to confirm multi-region LMN involvement
contraindicated_actions: Pursuing vascular workup (echocardiogram for emboli, angiography) as primary diagnostic strategy — course and bilateral multi-region findings inconsistent with cardiac embolic etiology
Stopping anticoagulation without cardiology input — AF stroke risk remains; ALS diagnosis does not change anticoagulation indication
Delaying swallowing evaluation — silent aspiration causing aspiration pneumonia is a leading cause of death in ALS
key_reasoning_points: Atrial fibrillation initially raised concern for vascular etiology but progressive 7-month bilateral course with fasciculations and hyperreflexia is inconsistent with embolic disease
MRI showing bilateral corticospinal tract changes extending from corona radiata to basis pontis is characteristic of ALS — not a vascular pattern
Bulbar-onset ALS has faster progression trajectory than limb-onset; elevated NfL >9,000 pg/mL confirms rapid degeneration
FVC at 68% and SNIP approaching threshold requires urgent NIV planning — PEG placement should be discussed and arranged before FVC falls below 50%
